meta.titre: Qualitative Analysis: flame tests and tests for ions and gases

sections.contenu_markdown: A technician testing river water in Limbe, a student in a school laboratory in Bafoussam and a forensic scientist in Yaounde all do the same thing: they identify unknown substances with simple tests. A flame that turns lilac, a white solid that appears when two clear liquids are mixed, a gas that turns limewater milky: each is a clue. The GCE O/L practical and theory papers ask you to complete tables of observations and inferences, to identify an unknown salt, and to describe the test for a gas. Accurate wording is what earns the marks, so this course shows what to write in each column.

items: A precipitate is an insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed.
A salt is made of a positive ion (cation) and a negative ion (anion).
An observation is what you see, hear or smell; an inference is the conclusion that it allows.
Limewater turns milky when carbon dioxide is passed through it.

sections.titre: Flame tests and tests for gases
sections.contenu_markdown:
Qualitative analysis uses simple tests to find out which substances are present. In every table write the **observation** (what you see) and the **inference** (what it shows). Never write an ion in the observation column.

**Flame test.** Clean a nichrome wire by dipping it in concentrated hydrochloric acid and heating it in a non-luminous Bunsen flame until it gives no colour. Dip the wire in the solid (moistened with acid) and hold it in the flame.

| Colour of the flame | Metal ion |
|---|---|
| crimson (red) | lithium, $\mathrm{Li^+}$ |
| golden yellow | sodium, $\mathrm{Na^+}$ |
| lilac | potassium, $\mathrm{K^+}$ |
| brick red | calcium, $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ |
| blue-green | copper(II), $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ |

**Tests for gases**

| Gas | Test | Positive result |
|---|---|---|
| Hydrogen | lighted splint | squeaky pop |
| Oxygen | glowing splint | splint relights |
| Carbon dioxide | limewater | turns milky |
| Ammonia | damp red litmus paper | turns blue |
| Chlorine | damp blue litmus paper | turns red, then is bleached |
| Sulphur dioxide | acidified potassium dichromate(VI) | orange turns green |

Carbon monoxide has no simple test with limewater. It is recognised because it burns with a blue flame and the product, carbon dioxide, turns limewater milky.

variantes.quand_utiliser: A question asks you to identify an anion.
variantes.contenu_markdown: **Carbonate:** add dilute hydrochloric acid. It fizzes and the gas turns limewater milky: $\mathrm{CO_{3}^{2-}(aq)\ +\ 2H^{+}(aq)  \rightarrow  H_{2}O(l)\ +\ CO_{2}(g)}$. **Sulphate:** add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution. A white precipitate shows sulphate: $\mathrm{Ba^{2+}(aq)\ +\ SO_{4}^{2-}(aq)  \rightarrow  BaSO_{4}(s)}$. The acid is added first because barium carbonate is also white but it dissolves in acid, whereas barium sulphate does not. **Chloride, bromide, iodide:** add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution: white, cream or yellow precipitate respectively.

variantes.quand_utiliser: A question gives observations with sodium hydroxide and ammonia solutions.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Add a few drops, then an excess, of each solution.

| Ion | Sodium hydroxide solution | Aqueous ammonia |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ | light blue precipitate, insoluble in excess | light blue precipitate, dissolves in excess to give a deep blue solution |
| $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ | green precipitate, insoluble in excess (turns brown on standing) | green precipitate, insoluble in excess |
| $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ | red-brown precipitate, insoluble in excess | red-brown precipitate, insoluble in excess |
| $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ | white precipitate, dissolves in excess | white precipitate, dissolves in excess |
| $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ | white precipitate, dissolves in excess | white precipitate, insoluble in excess |
| $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ | white precipitate, dissolves in excess | white precipitate, insoluble in excess |
| $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ | white precipitate, insoluble in excess | no precipitate, or only a very slight one |

Ammonium ions: warm with sodium hydroxide solution; ammonia gas is given off and turns damp red litmus paper blue. $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ are told apart with aqueous ammonia.

variantes.nom: Tests for water and for the -OH group
variantes.quand_utiliser: A question asks how to show that a liquid is water or an alcohol.
variantes.contenu_markdown: **Water:** anhydrous copper(II) sulphate turns from white to blue, and blue cobalt chloride paper turns pink. **Alcohols:** add phosphorus(V) chloride, $\mathrm{PCl_{5}}$. Misty (steamy) white fumes of hydrogen chloride are given off, for example $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}OH\ +\ PCl_{5}  \rightarrow  C_{2}H_{5}Cl\ +\ POCl_{3}\ +\ HCl}$. The same fumes appear with water, so the test shows the presence of -OH groups but must be done on a dry sample.

sections.enonce_markdown: Salt B forms pale green crystals that dissolve in water to give a pale green solution. Sodium hydroxide solution is added to one portion of this solution: a green precipitate forms which turns brown on standing, and it does not dissolve in excess. Dilute hydrochloric acid and then barium chloride solution are added to a second portion and a white precipitate forms. Identify B and write ionic equations for the two precipitates.

etapes.justification: A green precipitate that does not dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide, and turns brown on standing, is iron(II) hydroxide.

etapes.action: Write the equation for the first precipitate.
etapes.justification: Iron(II) ions and hydroxide ions combine to form an insoluble solid.
The acid is added first to remove carbonate. A white precipitate that remains with barium chloride shows sulphate.

etapes.action: Write the equation for the second precipitate and name B.
etapes.justification: Barium ions and sulphate ions combine to form insoluble barium sulphate.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $\mathrm{Ba^{2+}(aq)\ +\ SO_{4}^{2-}(aq)  \rightarrow  BaSO_{4}(s)}$ and B is iron(II) sulphate, $\mathrm{FeSO_{4}}$.

sections.conclusion_markdown: B is **iron(II) sulphate, FeSO4**: the cation is shown by the green precipitate that turns brown, and the anion by the white precipitate with acidified barium chloride.

items.erreur_markdown: Adding barium chloride solution alone, and concluding that a white precipitate is a sulphate.
items.pourquoi_faux: Carbonates and sulphites also give a white precipitate with barium chloride.
items.correction_markdown: Add dilute hydrochloric acid first. Only barium sulphate stays as a precipitate.

items.erreur_markdown: A lilac flame shows that sodium is present.
items.pourquoi_faux: Sodium gives a golden-yellow flame. Lilac is the flame colour of potassium.
items.correction_markdown: Golden yellow = sodium; lilac = potassium; brick red = calcium.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing "copper(II) ions present" in the observation column.
items.pourquoi_faux: An observation is only what you see. The name of the ion is an inference.
items.correction_markdown: Observation: light blue precipitate insoluble in excess. Inference: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ present.

items.erreur_markdown: The white precipitate from aluminium ions dissolves in excess aqueous ammonia.
items.pourquoi_faux: The aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide, but not in excess aqueous ammonia.
items.correction_markdown: Aluminium: white precipitate insoluble in excess ammonia. Zinc: white precipitate soluble in excess ammonia.

items.erreur_markdown: A gas that makes a lighted splint pop is oxygen.
items.pourquoi_faux: A squeaky pop is the test for hydrogen. Oxygen relights a glowing splint.
items.correction_markdown: Hydrogen: lighted splint gives a squeaky pop. Oxygen: glowing splint relights.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Name the metal ion that gives a golden-yellow flame.

(b) Name the metal ion that gives a brick-red flame.

(c) Describe the test for carbon dioxide and state the positive result.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Sodium** ($\mathrm{Na^+}$).

(b) **Calcium** ($\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$).

(c) Bubble the gas through limewater: the limewater turns **milky**.

items.enonce_markdown:
Solution C is colourless and solution D is blue. Their reactions are shown in the table.

| Test | Solution C | Solution D |
|---|---|---|
| Sodium hydroxide solution, drop by drop, then excess | white precipitate, dissolves in excess to give a colourless solution | light blue precipitate, insoluble in excess |
| Aqueous ammonia, drop by drop, then excess | white precipitate, dissolves in excess | light blue precipitate, dissolves in excess to give a deep blue solution |
| Dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution | white precipitate | no precipitate |

(a) Identify the cation in C and the cation in D.

(b) Identify the anion in C and name the compound C.

(c) Write an ionic equation for the white precipitate formed when sodium hydroxide solution is added to C.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) C contains $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ (a white precipitate that dissolves in excess of both reagents). D contains $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ (light blue precipitate that dissolves in excess ammonia to give a deep blue solution).

(b) A white precipitate with acidified silver nitrate shows chloride, $\mathrm{Cl^-}$, so C is **zinc chloride**.

(c) $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)\ +\ 2OH^{-}(aq)  \rightarrow  Zn(OH)_{2}(s)}$

items.enonce_markdown:
A white solid E is analysed. (i) When E is heated, a gas that turns limewater milky is given off, and the residue is yellow when hot and white when cold. (ii) E dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid with fizzing. Sodium hydroxide solution is added to the resulting solution: a white precipitate forms which dissolves in excess. (Zn = 65, C = 12, O = 16; molar volume = 24 $\mathrm{dm^3}$.)

(a) Identify E and write the equations for (i) and (ii).

(b) 12.5 g of E is heated until there is no more change. Calculate the mass of the residue and the volume of gas formed at room temperature and pressure.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The gas is carbon dioxide, so E is a carbonate. The yellow-when-hot, white-when-cold residue is zinc oxide, and the precipitate that dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide fits $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$. E is **zinc carbonate**, $\mathrm{ZnCO_{3}}$.

(i) $\mathrm{ZnCO_{3}  \rightarrow  ZnO\ +\ CO_{2}}$

(ii) $\mathrm{ZnCO_{3}\ +\ 2HCl  \rightarrow  ZnCl_{2}\ +\ H_{2}O\ +\ CO_{2}}$

(b) $M(\mathrm{ZnCO_3}) = 65 + 12 + 48 = 125$, so $n = \dfrac{12.5}{125} = 0.10\ \mathrm{mol}$. The ratio $\mathrm{ZnCO_3 : ZnO : CO_2}$ is 1 : 1 : 1. $M(\mathrm{ZnO}) = 81$, so the residue has mass $0.10 \times 81 = $ **8.1 g** and the gas has volume $0.10 \times 24 = $ **2.4 dm$^3$**.

items_markdown: Write the observation (what you see) and the inference (what it shows) in separate columns.
Flame colours: crimson Li, golden yellow Na, lilac K, brick red Ca, blue-green Cu.
Anions: carbonate (acid, limewater turns milky); sulphate (acid then barium chloride, white precipitate); halides (nitric acid then silver nitrate: white, cream, yellow).
Cations: use sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia, noting colour and whether the precipitate dissolves in excess.
Gas tests: hydrogen (pop), oxygen (relights glowing splint), carbon dioxide (limewater), ammonia (damp red litmus blue), chlorine (bleaches damp litmus).
Phosphorus(V) chloride gives misty fumes of hydrogen chloride with an alcohol.
